stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Each spring, collisions between warm Gulf air and cold continental air make the Great Plains one of the world's most active regions for severe weather. Towering as high as fifteen kilometers above the plains, ______ hail, lightning, and damaging winds within an hour of first appearing on radar.
choices: a cumulonimbus cloud, fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, often produce
the updrafts feeding a cumulonimbus cloud, which can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, often produce
a cumulonimbus cloud, fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, often produces
a cumulonimbus cloud is fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour, it often produces
explanation: Start by asking what is 'towering as high as fifteen kilometers above the plains.' It is the cloud, so the first noun after the comma has to be 'a cumulonimbus cloud.' Three choices pass that test, so finding the right subject is not enough. Next, check what follows it. The phrase 'fed by updrafts that can exceed 100 kilometers per hour' is an interrupter. If you cross it out, you get 'a cumulonimbus cloud... often produces.' A singular subject takes the singular verb 'produces.' The sentence also needs exactly one main clause, and this choice gives it one. Only C meets all three conditions: the right subject, a verb that agrees with it, and a sound sentence boundary.

A.why: You found the right subject, then let the plural nouns in the interrupter ('updrafts,' 'kilometers') set the verb. The subject is still the singular 'cloud,' so 'produce' doesn't agree with it. It needs 'produces.'

B.why: You chose a noun closely related to the cloud instead of the cloud itself. Updrafts are rising air inside the cloud, and they don't 'tower' fifteen kilometers above the plains. Because 'the updrafts' comes first after the comma, the opening phrase is left dangling.

D.why: The opening noun is right, but this choice joins two independent clauses ('a cumulonimbus cloud is fed...' and 'it often produces...') with only a comma. That's a comma splice. Getting the subject right doesn't make up for a broken sentence boundary.

subtype_name: Dangling modifier: who does the opening phrase describe?

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Folklorists classify traditional stories by their recurring plot elements rather than by their country of origin, since a single plot often crosses many borders. Passed orally from one generation of storytellers to the next for centuries before anyone wrote it down, ______ today in more than forty regional variants.
choices: collectors in at least six countries have documented the ferryman tale, which survives
the ferryman tale, documented by collectors in at least six countries, survives
the ferryman tale, documented by collectors in at least six countries, survive
the ferryman tale was documented by collectors in at least six countries, it survives
explanation: Ask what was 'passed orally from one generation of storytellers to the next.' It was the tale, so 'the ferryman tale' has to be the first noun after the comma. Three choices start that way, so you still have to check the rest of the clause. Cross out the interrupter 'documented by collectors in at least six countries' and you are left with 'the ferryman tale... survives.' That is a singular subject with a singular verb, and the sentence has one main clause. Only B gets the subject, the agreement, and the sentence structure right.

A.why: You started with the people connected to the story instead of the story itself. The collectors weren't 'passed orally' between generations; the tale was. With 'collectors' first, the opening phrase describes the wrong noun, even though the rest of the choice reads smoothly.

C.why: You picked the right subject, then matched the verb to the plural nouns just before the blank ('collectors,' 'countries'). The subject is the singular 'tale,' so it needs 'survives,' not 'survive.'

D.why: This choice starts with the right noun but creates two independent clauses, 'the ferryman tale was documented...' and 'it survives...', joined only by a comma. That's a comma splice, so the sentence fails even though the modifier attaches correctly.
